drills.q: Walk through the full memory hierarchy with real latency numbers from register to DRAM, and state the one ratio worth memorizing.
drills.a: Register ~0.3ns -> L1 ~4-5cyc/~1ns (32-48KB) -> L2 ~12-14cyc/~3-4ns (256KB-2MB) -> L3 ~40-75cyc/~10-20ns (tens of MB shared) -> local DRAM ~200-300cyc/~70-100ns -> remote NUMA DRAM (50-100% higher). The ratio worth memorizing: L1 hit vs DRAM access is roughly 100x in cycles.

drills.q: Define false sharing and name the perf tool and specific counter used to detect it in production.
drills.a: Two threads write to logically independent variables sharing one 64-byte cache line, so each write invalidates the whole line for the other core, forcing cross-core cache-to-cache transfers despite no real data contention. Detect with perf c2c record/report, looking for high HITM (hit-modified) counts.

drills.q: Why is padding the correct fix for false sharing, and why is reaching for a mutex or atomic the wrong fix?
drills.a: Padding (alignas(64), @Contended, manual struct padding) puts each variable on its own cache line, eliminating the coherence traffic at its source. A mutex/atomic is wrong because there is no actual data race -- the variables are logically independent; synchronizing them adds real overhead to solve a problem that doesn't require synchronization.

drills.q: Explain what a TLB miss costs and how huge pages address it, including the operational risk of the transparent variant.
drills.a: A TLB miss requires a page-table walk (4 levels on x86-64 for 4KB pages), costing ~100+ cycles on top of the actual data access -- comparable to or worse than an L2 miss. A 2MB huge page covers what would be 512 separate 4KB TLB entries, cutting miss rate for large working sets. Risk: Linux transparent huge pages use background compaction (khugepaged) that has caused documented latency spikes (notably Redis); explicit hugetlbfs avoids this for known large allocations.

drills.q: A dual-socket production host shows bimodal p99 latency not reproducible on single-socket test hardware. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Likely NUMA: threads and their memory ended up on different sockets (scheduler migration or allocation before pinning), so some accesses pay the remote-socket latency penalty (roughly 1.3-2x local) while others don't, producing bimodal latency. Confirm with numastat (cross-node access counts) and numactl --hardware; fix by pinning CPU and memory locality together (numactl --cpunodebind/--membind or runtime equivalent).

drills.q: State the four MESI states and trace what happens when one of three cores holding a Shared line writes to it.
drills.a: Modified (sole dirty owner), Exclusive (sole clean owner, silent upgrade to Modified on local write), Shared (multiple clean readers), Invalid (stale). On a write by one of three Shared holders: it broadcasts invalidation, its own copy goes Shared->Modified, the other two go Shared->Invalid; either of those cores touching the address again triggers a cache-to-cache transfer of the Modified copy.

drills.q: Explain associativity and describe a concrete access pattern that triggers pathological conflict misses.
drills.a: Associativity is how many distinct lines can occupy one cache set simultaneously; low associativity (e.g. direct-mapped) forces addresses hashing to the same set to repeatedly evict each other even with an otherwise-empty cache. A concrete trigger: striding through a large array with a stride that's a power-of-two multiple of the cache's set-mapping period (e.g. iterating columns of a power-of-two-sized matrix) causes nearly every access to land in the same set -- fixed by padding array dimensions or iterating in memory (row-major) order.

drills.q: Design a per-CPU counter/metrics array for a highly concurrent service. What layout eliminates coherence traffic, and what's the tradeoff if you instead need exact real-time consistency?
drills.a: One counter per logical CPU/thread, each padded to its own 64-byte cache line (hardware_destructive_interference_size), so every CPU writes its own line with zero cross-core invalidation; periodic reads sum across per-CPU slots, accepting eventual rather than immediate consistency. If exact, immediately-consistent totals are required, that conflicts with the lock-free design -- you'd need a single contended atomic (accepting real coherence cost) or a coarser synchronized snapshot; you cannot have zero contention and exact real-time consistency simultaneously.

drills.q: Compare the stacked cost of a TLB miss plus a NUMA-remote DRAM access against a fully-cached (TLB hit, L3 hit) access, and explain the practical tuning implication.
drills.a: A TLB miss (~100+ cycles for the page-table walk) happens before the data fetch; combined with a NUMA-remote DRAM miss (200-300+ cycles locally, 50-100% higher remote), a single logical access can exceed 500 cycles. A fully-cached access (TLB hit, L3 hit) costs on the order of tens of cycles. Implication: huge pages and NUMA pinning are paired tuning levers for large random-access workloads (databases, JVMs) -- adding more RAM fixes a capacity problem, not a cache/TLB miss latency problem.

drills.q: Why is a sequential array scan dramatically faster than pointer-chasing a linked list holding the same total data, independent of any cache-capacity difference?
drills.a: Sequential access amortizes each 64-byte cache line fetch across many useful bytes and lets the hardware prefetcher predict the stride and fetch ahead of demand. Pointer-chasing wastes most of each fetched line (nodes are scattered and often smaller than 64 bytes), defeats stride-based prefetching since the next address is data-dependent, and each hop can be a full latency-bound miss if the working set exceeds cache capacity -- a pure locality effect, not an algorithmic-complexity one.
